messages.subject: design of sampling units
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

We are surveying the population of guanacos (a large, wild ungulate)
in a 3600 km2 island-like peninsula in eastern Patagonia, aiming to
explain the variation in abundance due to habitat and human-related
factors. We surveyed 360 km of transects, using internal "roads"
(usually very bad, always surveyed using a 4WD pickup vehicle)
connecting different ranches across the area. In total, we traveled
along 12 different lines of variable length (between 9 and 70 km).
The explanatory factors (each with 3 levels) we are considering are:
habitat type, density of ranch-buildings and hunting pressure. Sheep
abundance will be an explanatory variable based on the estimates of
sheep encounter rate. The response variable will be guanaco encounter
rate.
As we will combine the factors with their different levels, this will
result in 9 different strata. Thus, we will consider the sampling
unit for a given stratum as the part of a long transect falling
within that stratum. Our problem is that the number of sampling units
per stratum will be too small in relation to the number of
explanatory variables/factors we want to test.
Questions are:
1. Is it valid to split the transect into smaller segments along a
line, and to consider these smaller segments as the new sampling
units?
If so, we may now face the problem of autocorrelation among the
sampling units placed along the same transect.
2. Is it possible to solve this problem by separating the new
sampling units, leaving blank spaces between them?
3. If this is ok, how can we detect and measure the autocorrelation
between smaller sampling units in order to decide their length and
the separation between contiguous units?

Any help/suggestions will be very much appreciated-

Ricardo

messages.subject: covariate detection probabilities
messages.body_plain:
Hello List,

I am a new DISTANCE user so please forgive my ignorance.

I am using multiple covariate distance sampling model to obtain
probabilities of detection at different Beaufort Sea States (0-4) along a
trackline. I have managed to import the data correctly and run analyses
without errors. However, I cannot get the detection probabilities for each
sea state at different distances out of the results. The plots visually
describe the data I want, but I can't seem to get the values. Is my only
chance to plug distance values into each function of each sea state? If so,
I would appreciate any guidance on that step.

Thank you all so much for any advice. Please send email responses to
lg...@duke.edu.

Cheers,
Leigh

Leigh Torres
PhD Candidate
Duke University Marine Lab
Beaufort, NC 28516
lg...@duke.edu

messages.subject: Re: covariate detection probabilities
messages.body_plain:
Hi Leigh, list,

It is quite easy to get estimated detection probability at a given distance:

(A)You can get the actual values used in the plots in one of two ways:
- (1) When a plot is showing in the analysis details window, right click and
choose "Copy plot to clipboard", or click on the "Copy current window to
clipboard" button on the main toolbar.  Then open a text file or a spreadsheet
and do a paste.
- (2) In the model definition properties, under Detection Function |
Diagnostics, tick the button to "Create file of histogram data".
To find out what the various columns mean, look in the online help index under
"Plot file".

(B) You can also work out the value by hand, using the parameter estimates, as
you indicate.  For more about this, and a worked example, look in the online
help index under "Detection Function" | "About formulae".

Another thing you might want is an estimate of average probability of
detection within the surveyed area (ie between 0 and w, the truncation
distance).  This is a bit harder and unfortunately Distance doesn't give it
for each level of a factor covariate.  One approach would be to take the
average of the values output from the plotting functions, above.  A more
accurate approach would be to use a stats or maths package to integrate the
detection function using the parameter estimate values given by Distance.
There is a bit about this in the online topic "Calculating effective strip
width", which is the page after the one that tells you about calculating
detection function formulae (reall that average probability of detection is
effective strip width over trucation distance, for line transects).

Hope this helps,

 - Len

--

messages.subject: Announce: Workshops, St Andrews, Summer 2006
messages.body_plain:
-----------------------------------------------------------------------
Centre for Research into Ecological and Environmental Modelling (CREEM)
University of St Andrews, St Andrews, Scotland

International Training Workshops in
Distance Sampling Methods for
Wildlife Population Assessment

http://www.creem.st-and.ac.uk/conferences.php
-----------------------------------------------------------------------

Registration for the following workshops is now open - see web site for
details.  Note that we are also holding an introductory workshop in New
Zealand in June 2006 - again, see web site for details.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------

Workshop 1: Introduction to Distance Sampling

This 3-day workshop will give participants a solid grounding in the basic
methods for design and analysis of distance sampling surveys for estimating
the density and/or abundance of wildlife populations. It is a blend of
theory and practice, and participants will learn how to use the industry-
standard program Distance.  We will focus on "conventional" distance
sampling methods, as described in the standard reference book "Introduction
to Distance Sampling".

Workshop 2: Advanced Distance Sampling

This 2.5-day workshop will cover recent advances in distance sampling
research and software, as described in the book "Advanced Distance
Sampling". It is intended for those already familiar with conventional
distance sampling methods.  We will teach advanced material such as
automated survey design, adaptive sampling, incorporating covariates into
the detection function and methods for where g(0)<1. Participants will learn
the more advanced features of Distance.  Note that this workshop is
naturally complemented by the subsequent workshop on density surface
modelling.

Workshop 3: Primer on Density Surface Modelling from Distance Sampling Data

This new, 2.5-day workshop will focus on methods of predicting abundance or
density of biological data using the  count  method of Hedley and Buckland
(2004, Chapter 4 of "Advanced Distance Sampling"). Variation in animal
density/abundance is modelled as functions of covariates such as land cover
type, habitat, bathymetry, altitude or depth. General additive models (GAMs)
or general linear models (GLMs) will be fitted to estimated densities along
transects using a new analytical engine inside program Distance. This is an
advanced workshop for those already familiar with distance sampling.
Participants intending to model their own data will be required to have it
formatted according to precise specifications prior to arrival at St.
Andrews.

The workshops are aimed at wildlife managers, ecologists and statisticians.
All feature a mix of lectures and hands-on computer sessions.  They are
taught by leading researchers from the Centre for Research into Ecological
and Environmental Modelling (CREEM) at St Andrews..

For more details, please see http://www.creem.st-and.ac.uk/conferences.php
or contact Rhona Rodger, Workshop Organizer, CREEM, University of St
Andrews, The Observatory, St. Andrews, Scotland KY16 9LZ. Tel:+44 1334
461842. Fax: +44 1334 461800. Email: rh...@mcs.st-and.ac.uk

--

messages.subject: Re: design of sampling units
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ricardo, list,

What you are proposing (post-stratifing the transects into many strata, each
of which has a unique combination of the factors of interest) is a design-
based approach to answering your question.  It is not an ideal approach in
your case for several reasons:
- the transects were not laid down at random- you have few transects and
relatively little survey effort
- there are several factors, so there will be many strata each of which will
contain little (or maybe no) survey effort
- the analysis will be complex as you will need to deal with correlation
between strata due to splitting the same transects into different strata

Instead, can I suggest you take a model-based approach, where you construct
a statistical model to explain density/abundance in terms of the factors of
interest.  A model based approach doesn't make any assumption about the
design, so non-random transects are not necessarily a problem (although they
can cause other issues such as non-uniform distribution of animals with
respect to the transect line).  Model selection methods also allow you to
directly address the question of interest: what factors affect animal
density.  One downside is that the analysis methods are not simple.

Some approaches to model-basd estimation are given in Chapter 4 of the
Advanced Distance Sampling book, and also in
Hedley, S.L., Buckland, S.T. and Borchers, D.L. 1999. Spatial modelling from
line transect data. Journal of Cetacean Research and Management 1, 255-264.

We are currently developing an analysis engine in Distance that implements
the "count" method described in the book chapter, and will provide training
on this method and a beta version of the analysis engine in our up-coming
workshop at St Andrews this summer "Primer on Density Surface Modelling from
Distance Sampling Data" - for more on this, see
http://www.ruwpa.st-and.ac.uk/distance.workshops/
We don't have a timetable for a public release of the new analysis engine
yet I'm afraid.

Others are using and developing similar approaches (which are also sometimes
called "spatial modelling" or "density surface modelling") - for some clues
try searching the distance-sampling list using the key word "spatial".

Hope this helps,

 - Len
